tur46-1: Follow-up period in one trial that found no meaningful difference between wait-and-see, heel inserts and physiotherapy
tur46-2: Small studies suggest that gel heel cups and shock-absorbing insoles may reduce pain in the short term; the evidence is limited. In a trial of 124 children, all groups improved clearly within 2 months; shock-absorbing heel inserts gave a small, clinically unimportant extra benefit over prefabricated insoles, and changing shoes made no difference. This trial had no untreated comparison group.
tur46-3: In a trial of 101 children, there was no meaningful difference at 3 months between wait-and-see (taking a break from painful activities), a heel-raise insert and physiotherapist-supervised eccentric calf exercises. At 6 weeks, the children using the heel insert were the most satisfied group; heel pain decreased clearly in all three groups. So most children get better with simple measures. If the pain does not go away or keeps coming back, an individual assessment can help.
tur46-4: Is your child saying that the bump just below the knee hurts after football, basketball or running? Osgood-Schlatter occurs in active children and teenagers during a growth spurt, when the front thigh muscle repeatedly pulls, through the kneecap tendon, on the growing end of the shinbone. Although it can look worrying, in most children it goes away once growth is complete; in some, however, knee pain can last for years. With well-adjusted activity and exercise, most children can get through this period without giving up their sport completely, cutting back for a while if needed.
tur46-5: Teenagers reporting improvement after a 12-week activity-adjustment and strengthening programme (51 participants, study without a control group)
tur46-6: Usually they do not need to stop completely. Sport is not expected to cause permanent damage, but it can increase the pain. Until the pain is under control, it is advisable to reduce the duration, frequency and total amount of demanding activities, especially running and jumping. If the pain is very severe, a complete break may be needed for a while.
tur46-7: The pain often eases within a few months, but some symptoms can last 12–24 months. It usually goes away once bone growth is complete. It can flare up again during a new growth spurt or with intense sport. But it is not always short-lived: in Denmark, among 43 people (aged 14–55 at the time) who answered a survey a median of 3.75 years (2–6 years) after diagnosis, 60% still had knee pain, and those with pain had a lower quality of life; the low survey response rate may have affected the result.
tur46-8: In a study of 51 young people aged 10–14, 80% reported improvement after a 12-week programme made up of a pain-guided activity ladder, knee strengthening and a gradual return to sport; at 12 months 69% had returned to sport. Because the study had no control group, the results should be interpreted with caution, but it may be an alternative to simply resting and waiting.
tur46-9: Total score of the Beighton examination, which assesses joint mobility
tur46-10: International threshold score for adults up to age 50 (4 over 50; 6 in pre-pubertal children and adolescents)
tur46-11: Reported frequency of joint hypermobility syndrome/hEDS among adults attending outpatient physiotherapy with musculoskeletal complaints
tur46-12: No. Many people with flexible joints have no complaints at all. In some people, however, flexibility comes with pain, frequent sprains or dislocations, and fatigue; today this is called hypermobility spectrum disorder, or hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) if specific criteria are met (formerly: joint hypermobility syndrome).
tur46-13: It is a simple 9-point examination doctors use to assess joint mobility: bending the little finger back beyond 90 degrees, touching the thumb to the forearm, the elbow and the knee bending backwards more than 10 degrees (one point each for right and left), and placing the palms flat on the floor with the knees straight (one point). Under the 2017 international criteria, the threshold for generalised joint hypermobility is 6 in pre-pubertal children and adolescents, 5 in adults up to age 50 and 4 over age 50. It is not a self-diagnosis test; the diagnosis is made by a doctor.
tur46-14: The evidence is limited but promising. In a small number of studies, pain decreased and strength increased after exercise programmes; however, it has not yet been shown that exercise is better than a control group, or which type of exercise is best. That is why the programme is tailored to the person and built up gradually. A 2024 review of 4 studies (exercise programmes, taping and compression orthoses) in hypermobile adults with shoulder complaints found positive changes over time in pain, shoulder instability, daily activities and muscle strength; however, information on the most effective type and dose of exercise is still lacking.
